annotations.keyFindings: Antibiotic prescribing fell from 61 to 38 percent with the decision aid against 60 to 55 percent with usual care; admissions for dental infection 0.4 versus 0.5 percent; intracluster correlation 0.06.
annotations.limitations: Self-selected practices with better dental access than average.

annotations.keyFindings: Six small placebo-controlled trials (412 participants): antibiotics did not reduce pain or swelling at 24 or 72 hours when dental treatment was given.
annotations.limitations: Small trials; no trial of people without access to dental treatment.

annotations.keyFindings: A triage line took 1,140 calls in its first year; 62 percent of callers were booked for urgent dental care within 48 hours and antibiotics were advised for 9 percent.
annotations.limitations: Conference abstract; year of the data, number of practices and follow-up not reported.
annotations.notes: Too little reported to rate relevance, quality or certainty; left unrated.

annotations.keyFindings: Recommends analgesia and dental referral for toothache without swelling, and antibiotics only for spreading infection, systemic signs or infection without access to urgent dental treatment.
annotations.limitations: Undated leaflet with no listed evidence sources.
annotations.notes: Not a study; no scores given.

annotations.keyFindings: 38 percent of adults in the most deprived fifth had no regular dentist against 17 percent in the least deprived fifth; those without a dentist consulted GPs for dental pain three times as often.
21 GPs prescribed because patients could not get dental care, for fear of missing spreading infection and because of patient expectation; they wanted same-day dental advice and a short decision aid.
Emergency attendances for dental infection rose 24 percent as dental access fell; admissions for spreading infection about 0.3 per 10,000 adults per year.

claims.text: In a cluster randomised trial in 24 practices, antibiotic prescribing for dental pain fell from 61 to 38 percent with a decision aid and urgent dental advice, against 60 to 55 percent with usual care.
claims.passage: antibiotic prescribing fell from 61 to 38 percent in intervention practices and from 60 to 55 percent in control practices
claims.interpretation: A reduction of this size is plausible for the local pathway; the trial's practices had better dental access.

claims.text: Hospital admissions for dental infection within 14 days were 0.4 percent with the decision aid and 0.5 percent with usual care.
claims.passage: Hospital admissions for dental infection within 14 days were 0.4 percent in intervention practices and 0.5 percent in control practices.
claims.interpretation: No signal of harm, but admissions are too rare for one trial to exclude it; a balancing measure is needed.

claims.text: When dental treatment was also provided, antibiotics did not reduce toothache or swelling compared with placebo at 24 or 72 hours.
claims.passage: When dental treatment was also provided, antibiotics did not reduce pain or swelling compared with placebo at 24 or 72 hours.
claims.interpretation: Supports reserving antibiotics, conditional on access to dental treatment, which the triage line provides.

claims.text: General practitioners said they prescribed antibiotics for toothache because patients could not get dental care or for fear of missing a spreading infection, and asked for same-day dental advice.
claims.passage: Doctors wanted a direct route to same-day dental advice and a short decision aid that fitted into a ten-minute consultation.
claims.interpretation: The pathway targets the stated reasons for prescribing.

claims.text: In the first year of a same-day dental telephone triage line, 62 percent of callers were booked for urgent dental care within 48 hours.
claims.passage: Dental nurses booked 62 percent of callers for urgent dental care within 48 hours
claims.interpretation: Indicates the triage line can work; high uncertainty because the source is an undated conference abstract left unrated.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two have no stated year and were left unrated. A cluster randomised trial found that a decision aid with urgent dental advice lowered antibiotic prescribing for dental pain without more admissions for dental infection, and a review of placebo-controlled trials found no benefit of antibiotics when dental treatment was given. General practitioners prescribe mainly because patients cannot reach dental care, a problem concentrated in deprived neighbourhoods. A triage line booked most callers for urgent care in one service report whose date and follow-up are unknown. Evidence supports testing the pathway locally with a safety balancing measure.
gradeRationale: One cluster randomised trial in better-served practices and a review of small trials; indirect to a district with poor dental access; two sources undated and unrated.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; two left unrated with unknown year; five claims; certainty low.
